rv.q: It worries so much about keeping you entertained it barely leaves a mark.

But no matter how much of a nerd you are for international cooperation and eco activism, this play by Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson labors in vain to fashion art from meetings mired in the language of bureaucratic minutiae.
In the skilled hands of co-directors Stephen Daldry and Justin Martin, a complex scientific and historical topic has been transformed into a riveting runaway thriller.
Kyoto is an exciting, enrapturing theatrical spectacle.
The performances and rapid-fire timing throughout are rock solid, a thrill ride from start to end.
That makes Kyoto, Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson’s electrifying political thriller about climate diplomacy in the 1990s, an impressive feat.
Matter-of-fact in an appealing way, sometimes witty, he can be almost persuasive at first when he argues that the science is not clear...
It is fast-paced, loaded with information, and a true ensemble vehicle that uses each inch of designer Miriam Buether’s set to bring audience members closer to the action.
Despite its grand scope and impressive pedigree, this Off-Broadway import from the Royal Shakespeare Company ultimately feels more didactic than dramatic.

While Kyoto offers striking scenes and moments, often staged at a quick clip by its directors, the play remains a weighty work that’s not always engrossing in spite of the excellence of its actors, who do plenty of heavy lifting to keep it moving along.
Otherwise, watching these debates about climate over a conference table is about as riveting as watching anything that goes on at the United Nations.
A remarkable work, not to be missed!
Kyoto offers lessons in the rewards that can come from even such fitful advances.
The production’s precision, its layered use of sound and video, its flashes of genuine wit, all dutifully build toward a final formula that feels both hopeless and completely human.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this climate-change drama about the Kyoto Protocol negotiations. Many praise its ambition and riveting ensemble work, but others find it overlong and more lecture than drama, with shallow execution beneath slick production.

vr.q: It's a well-crafted piece of political theater about climate diplomacy which is so urgent right now.
I would say this is a good play in that it got me to think.
